subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
passage: The biology presentation was due Monday, in the same week as three unit tests. Shreya and Nazia had split it: Shreya the slides, Nazia the research. On Thursday Shreya thought, Nazia's so careful, she'll probably cover the slides too. I'll study for chemistry. On Friday, with the power cutting out every evening, Nazia thought, Shreya's quick, she'll probably pull the research off the internet with the slides. I'll do maths. On Sunday night each opened the shared file. It had a title and nothing else. By midnight they had pulled together a messy seven slides. On Monday the teacher gave them a C and wrote, "You two can do far better than this." Both had done well in their tests. Neither felt good.

qa.q: How many slides did they pull together by midnight?
qa.a: A messy seven slides.

qa.q: Why did it feel safe to Shreya to switch to chemistry on Thursday?
qa.a: Shreya felt reassured, trusting that careful Nazia would probably cover the slides too, so studying chemistry seemed to cost nothing.

qa.q: What could they have done on Thursday to avoid Sunday night?
qa.a: A quick check-in on the shared file, so each would see the other's plan and neither could assume the other would cover.

qa.q: How might the teacher see their C?
qa.a: The teacher saw two capable students producing weak work, and wrote that they can do far better, sensing effort was missing.

grounding: Two teenagers each skip their part of a joint presentation expecting the other to cover, so both end up worse off than if they had cooperated.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
passage: At the tuition centre in Chembur, Francis and Ankita were paired for a ten-minute history talk on the salt march. They agreed to rehearse on Tuesday and Thursday. On Tuesday Ankita messaged, "Can't come, cousin's engagement. You're so good at speaking, you'll manage." Francis felt a small relief. If Ankita wasn't bothering, why should he? On Thursday he skipped too, telling himself Ankita would read up at home. On Saturday they stood before the class with one printed page each. Francis forgot the dates. Ankita lost her place twice. The talk lasted four minutes. Afterwards, on the stairs, Ankita said, "I thought you'd carry it." Francis said, "I thought you would." They both laughed, but not happily.

qa.q: How long did their talk last?
qa.a: Four minutes.

qa.q: Why did Francis feel a small relief at Ankita's message?
qa.a: He took it as permission to skip too, thinking that if Ankita wasn't bothering, he needn't either.

qa.q: Where did things go wrong, and what could Francis have done at that point?
qa.a: At Thursday's rehearsal; Francis could have messaged Ankita to fix a new time instead of assuming she would read up at home.

qa.q: What is it like for Ankita on the stairs when Francis says 'I thought you would'?
qa.a: Ankita realises they both counted on the other, and feels embarrassed and let down by both of them.

grounding: Two teenagers preparing a talk each skip rehearsal expecting the other to carry it, and the joint result is worse for both.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
passage: "Did you do the survey part?" Rehana asked in the school library, dropping her bag. "Me? I thought you were doing it." Zainab looked up from her notes. "We said we'd both do it." "Yes, but you always overdo things. I figured you'd finish it anyway." "And I figured you'd feel guilty and finish it." They stared at each other. "So nobody asked the thirty students." "Nobody asked anybody." "It's due at two." Zainab checked the clock. "It's twelve-forty." "If we'd each done fifteen, it'd be done." "And instead we each did zero." Rehana sat down hard. "Okay. You take the canteen, I'll take the field. Fifteen each. Go." They ran.

qa.q: How many students were they supposed to survey?
qa.a: Thirty students.

qa.q: What did Rehana expect Zainab to do, and why?
qa.a: Rehana felt confident Zainab would finish the survey anyway, because Zainab always overdoes things.

qa.q: What choice did they make at twelve-forty, and why was it better?
qa.a: They split the survey fifteen each, canteen and field, so each did a clear part instead of waiting for the other.

qa.q: How does Zainab's reason for skipping mirror Rehana's?
qa.a: Zainab figured Rehana would feel guilty and finish it, the same bet Rehana made, so both lost.

grounding: Two teenagers each leave a joint survey to the other, so neither does it, and they end up rushing when a fair split would have left both better off.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
passage: I'm Parveen. In Class 11, Gurleen and I were paired to present a working water-filter model at the school exhibition. We were both good students, which was the problem. I thought, Gurleen loves building things, she'll make it. I'll prepare the speech on the night before. Gurleen, I found out later, thought, Parveen is so organised, she'll make sure it's done. Each of us made the choice that seemed smartest for ourselves. Two days before, we finally met with a bucket of sand, a cut bottle and no plan. The model leaked in front of the judges, onto the principal's shoes. We got a participation certificate. What stung was knowing that if we'd both worked, even half as hard as usual, we would have done well.

qa.q: What happened to the water-filter model in front of the judges?
qa.a: It leaked, onto the principal's shoes.

qa.q: What did Parveen think about Gurleen before the exhibition?
qa.a: She thought Gurleen loves building things and would make the model, so Parveen could leave her own part until the night before.

qa.q: What choice would have changed the result for both girls?
qa.a: If each had done her own agreed part early instead of counting on the other, even half-hearted work together would have beaten the leaking model.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel when she learns what Parveen had been thinking?
qa.a: She might feel a little annoyed but also recognise herself, since she had made the same bet about Parveen.

grounding: Two teenage girls each shirk their joint exhibition work expecting the other to cover, and both end up worse off than if they had cooperated.

subtopic: Prisoner's dilemma and cooperation vs defection
passage:
Debate coach's note, Friday. Written by Kishore Sir.

Ujjwal and Hemlata, both Class 12, were partners in today's inter-house debate. Last week they agreed Ujjwal would prepare rebuttals and Hemlata the opening. Today the opening was thin and there were no rebuttals at all. They lost to the house that came fourth last year.

Afterwards I spoke to each alone. Ujjwal said, "She always over-prepares, Sir. I thought she'd cover the rebuttals too." Hemlata said, "He's good at thinking on his feet. I thought he'd carry it if I did less." Both looked miserable, and a little angry with each other.

My next step: on Monday I'll sit them down together, show them both answers side by side, and have them write their parts on one sheet with dates.

qa.q: Which parts had Ujjwal and Hemlata agreed to prepare?
qa.a: Ujjwal would prepare the rebuttals and Hemlata the opening.

qa.q: What did each partner think about the other before the debate?
qa.a: Each felt relaxed about doing less, trusting the other to cover: Ujjwal assumed Hemlata would over-prepare, and Hemlata assumed Ujjwal would carry it on his feet.

qa.q: Why is showing them both answers side by side a useful next step?
qa.a: Seeing that each made the same bet would help them understand that both shirking made both lose, and writing parts with dates makes each accountable.

qa.q: How does the loss look to the rival house that won?
qa.a: They may be pleasantly surprised to beat a strong pair, not knowing the pair lost because each left the work to the other.

grounding: Two teenage debate partners each do less expecting the other to cover, so both lose, as recorded by their coach.
